posts.title: Intents, not shell translation
posts.description: One playbook should name what you want. PlayTime binds how on this computer. Equivalence Engine is a catalog -- not a blender that turns bash into PowerShell.
posts.html:
You have a setup document that works on your laptop.

Your teammate opens it on Windows. You start swapping apt for winget. Quotes explode. Paths lie. && becomes a ghost. You now own two documents that pretend to be the same procedure.

That urge is honest. The overall process usually is the same: detect, acquire, configure, verify. The trap is treating "the same procedure" as "hot-replace inside a bash file."

We are not building a shell compiler. We do not have one. We should not pretend Equivalence Engine is one.

Write what you want. At play time, the machine binds how for this computer.

Figure 1. Cookbook, kitchen, waiter

Call the file format CentrMark (.cmk). It is only writing. A playbook directive means nothing until a profile gives it a job.

Call the engine PlayTime. That name fell out of the phrase "at play time" and then earned a layer. PlayTime reads the book, learns the host, asks Equivalence Engine for a command, runs it, and writes a sidecar next to the file. It never rewrites the recipe.

Call the app Scriptbook. Today that is a CLI. Later it is also a DevCentr screen. It opens the book and talks to you. It must not become a second resolver.

The book is not the kitchen. The kitchen is not the waiter. Mixing those three is how Equivalence Engine grows a document runner, and how Scriptbook grows a package catalog. We already have both of those, elsewhere.

The blender we refused

Equivalence Engine already has two machines. People mash them together because they share a logo.

code is a path: library 5.15 → 6.0, apply rewrites. That is the "equivalence" story people remember.

cli and filesystem are already lookups. cli.install gh plus a host key returns a row in a catalog. There is no migration path from winget to apt. There is a table.

If we stuffed format and shell into that path — windows/winget/pwsh/msi — we would tensor two independent facts into nodes. The lattice would eat the engine. That is the hairy version. We did not take it.

Figure 2. Do not put a bash script through a blender

winget install GitHub.cli is not a bash program. It is not a pwsh program. It is argv: a program name and some arguments. Spawn it with no shell, the way a GUI button would. Then you do not need three "equivalent" rows for three coats.

Figure 3. One suitcase, no costumes

Shell still exists. Scriptbook’s shell= is for glue cells — echo, a Nushell helper, the verify step that is already portable. Catalog rows stay runtime argv unless the method really is curl | bash. That is a constraint ("this host must have bash"), not a dimension we multiply by format.

The student asked: MSI or bash?

Figure 4. Two doors is not a questionnaire

The teacher did not open either door. That is not a choice.

Same spine, different satellites

Install a CLI. Put config in the user config dir. Open port 443. Enable a background service. The graph is the same. The command bound to each node is not.

Sometimes the method grows extra steps that hang off the acquire node. AppImage wants a desktop file. MSI wants elevation. Flatpak does not want PATH surgery. That is a choice node that expands a small subgraph — not a second playbook.

Ask only the overlap: this tool’s methods on this host. If the overlap is one method, do not ask.

Figure 5. Ask only the overlap

GPU drivers and "tray app vs Windows service" are the exceptions. Do not force one graph there. Do not make the exception the engine.

The cycle that looked real

We wanted to register abstract instructions in Equivalence Engine so PlayTime could dereference them later. That is right. cli.install already is one. os.version would be another.

Then: if "find the OS version" is an intent, how does the engine pick the method for "find the OS version" without knowing the OS?

It doesn’t. That loop is real, and we do not walk it.

PlayTime is a compiled program. It already knows NT vs not. It probes PATH without shelling out to where versus which (those commands assume an OS). It freezes a Host Identity Record. Nested expansions reuse that snapshot. They do not re-detect and disagree.

os.version as a later playbook step is an ordinary dereference: print the version string, filtered by the snapshot you already have. PowerShell-on-Linux does not save the first step. $IsLinux only works if you are already inside pwsh. PlayTime is not.

Figure 6. Snapshot, then dereference

Call the bootstrap contract Host Awareness. There is no vendor get_os(). There are cousins: uname, /etc/os-release, RtlGetVersion, sw_vers. We sit on those. A hobby kernel can fill the record. Microsoft will not file a PR; we still bake a Windows probe.

WSL is not a new planet. It is Linux with a sticker.

The loop we actually wanted

CI already compiles tools.sdl to tools.json. Aim that trick at stage zero.

Humans register probe rows and intents in shared rules. CI runs Equivalence Engine as a compiler — it does not detect the GitHub runner — and writes an ordered cascade into PlayTime. The shipped binary wakes up offline. After the record exists, runtime PlayTime may call the engine for cli.install. New row → next bake → next release.

That is a ratchet, not a deadlock. Catalogs get richer. PlayTime wakes up on more machines. People write more playbooks. They register more intents. The next bake is richer.

Figure 7. Ratchet at build time

You live in the attic. You write install gh. The basement is argv. When winget flags change, you rewrite the basement. The book does not move. Because that is cheap, you write more abstract scripts instead of more shell. Vocabulary grows up. Realizations stay down.

Figure 8. Attic intents, basement argv

PlayTime sounds like an OpenShellOrg concern: argv honesty, host identity, not lying about which process you spawned. It might belong there someday. It is being built in scriptbook right now. We are not relocating the kitchen mid-service.

Figure 9. Aligned, not moved

The details — directives, sidecar fields, probe kinds, --to must stay a host alias — live in the docs. This page is the orientation: intents, not shell translation. Same book. This computer fills in the verbs.

  • Abstract playbooks (encyclopedia)

  • scriptbook · PlayTime at the shell boundary

posts.title: When a Cloud project pretends to be an app
posts.description: Google Cloud forces personal OAuth into Project-shaped boxes—consent, quotas, and API enablement included. Here is the mental model we document instead.
posts.html:
You do not think in Google Cloud Projects.

You think: this is my account, these are the apps I trust, this one may read Drive, that one may sync files. Composio asks for a Client ID and Client Secret. rclone already has one. The Console shrugs and hands you another Project wizard—same enterprise path you would use for a billing account and a fleet of VMs.

That is not a small UX annoyance. It is a noun collision. Consent screens, enabled APIs, and quotas hang off the Project. OAuth Client IDs are children of it. Two Client IDs in one Project do not give you two apps; they give you two credential strings sharing one consent name, one scope union, and one rate-limit bucket. Revoke the “app” and you may have revoked more than you meant.

We wrote the Dev-Centr docs the way people actually learn this:

  • A how-to that stays task-shaped—pick a trust boundary, create the Project as a stand-in for that boundary, enable the real API (Drive, not Enterprise Notebooks), leave JavaScript origins empty when you only need a redirect URI, reuse one Client ID when you want one Composio trust platform, re-authorize after scope growth.

  • An explanation that shows the ideal model, the actual coupling, and the map between them—with diagrams, not a lecture stuffed into the how-to.

  • A reference concept map for when you are mid-Console and need the noun table.

The opinion underneath: keep calling them apps in your head. Label Projects as trust platforms, not “Personal 2.0” folders. Lump when you want one revoke story (all Google toolkits inside Composio). Split when the products are different (Composio vs rclone). Do not pretend a second Client ID is isolation.

Longer treatment lives in General Knowledge—start at the explanation if you want the pictures, or the how-to if you are already holding the Client Secret dialog.

  • Google Cloud projects as OAuth boundaries

  • Set up Google Cloud OAuth for personal tools

  • Concept map

posts.title: When API keys wear token costumes
posts.description: Vendors keep labeling long-lived dashboard secrets as tokens. Here is the architectural split Dev-Centr is forcing into docs and Secrets Manager—and why the wrong word keeps breaking security reviews.
posts.html:
Open almost any developer console and you will find the same soft lie waiting under a friendly button: Generate your API access token. You click it. You get a long string that never expires unless you delete it, that identifies your project or account, and that you will paste into a .env file and forget until something leaks. That string is not an access token in the OAuth sense. It is an API key wearing a costume stitched from marketing and Bearer-header habits.

We are done pretending the costume is the thing. Dev-Centr’s docs and Secrets Manager now name credentials by what they do, not by what the vendor’s UI whispered while you were trying to ship.

Practitioner lock (use this in reviews and agent prompts): API key vs token. Product enforcement: Secrets Manager vocabulary.

A scene from every onboarding

Picture a Monday standup where someone says the integration is "using a token." Half the room hears short-lived OAuth bearer from a login flow. The other half hears the string we copied from Settings → Developers last quarter. Nobody notices the mismatch until a rotation runbook says "revoke the key" and an agent helpfully tries to refresh it like a session.

That is not pedantry. Wrong nouns pick the wrong playbook: dashboard rotate versus protocol refresh; project metering versus user consent; forever-secret versus fifteen-minute claim set.

What the words actually mean

An API key identifies the application or project making the request. It is how a platform bills you, rates you, and attributes traffic to "the Stripe integration" or "the mobile backend." It does not prove which human is pressing the buttons inside that app.

An access token—OAuth access token, JWT bearer, session token—identifies an authorized subject for a limited time. It answers what this holder may do now, often with scopes and an expiry baked into the credential (or into the introspection service behind it).

Hold the analogies for a second and you can feel the difference in your hands:

  • The API key is the project’s driver’s license. The meter knows which fleet car pulled up.

  • The access token is a hotel keycard. It opens these floors for this stay. Morning checkout is a feature, not a bug.

How "token" ate the dashboard

OAuth taught a generation of engineers that scoped access arrives as an access token. Cloud consoles borrowed the word for a different product: long-lived secrets you mint yourself, optionally with checkbox scopes, optionally revoked one-by-one without nuking the whole account.

So the industry grew a middle creature—scoped API keys, often sold as personal access tokens (PATs)—and dressed it in token language because:

  • scopes made it feel like OAuth,

  • Bearer headers made it travel like OAuth,

  • and "token" sounded newer and safer than the grim old "API key" that once meant a single immortal string for the entire account.

Useful product evolution. Terrible vocabulary.

Under the hood you still have two architectures:

  • Scoped key / PAT — long-lived, dashboard-born, manually revoked, project- or account-bound with capability limits.

  • True access token — handshake-born, short TTL, subject-bound, refreshed by protocol rather than by a human with a clipboard.

The rule we are enforcing

Ignore the button. Ask three questions:

  1. Was this pasted from a settings page, or minted by a login / client-credentials handshake?

  2. Does it expire in minutes or hours by design, or only when someone deletes it?

  3. Does it authorize a user or session, or only identify a project for metering?

Dashboard paste + manual revoke → API key (scoped or not). Handshake + TTL → access token (and keep refresh token for the minting secret, not for ordinary API calls).

In Secrets Manager kinds we write that as api_key, scoped_api_key, access_token, and refresh_token. Vendor aliases can live in notes for search. They do not get to own the type field.

Why Dev-Centr is picking this fight

We distribute secrets for a living—vendor → vault → local env → hosting matrix—and agents already hallucinate env names when the nouns wobble. If the UI says "token" and the architecture says "key," the agent will under-rotate forever-strings or over-store live session material. Security reviews then argue about words instead of blast radius.

So the docs tell the truth, the product forces the kinds, and this post is the public notice: stop calling keys tokens just because a dashboard did.

The costume can stay on the marketing site. It does not get into our registry.

posts.title: Business Bootstrap becomes a support-systems hub
posts.description: Founder ops docs grow past email—scheduling, design, and vaults get their own capability areas on docs.devcentr.org.
posts.html:
Business Bootstrap on docs.devcentr.org is no longer just the email matrix and org infra pattern. It is a support-systems hub: Email, Scheduling, Design, Vault, and Org infra—each with room for explanation, how-tos, and interconnect notes.

What landed first under the new shape:

  • Scheduling — Cal.com (hosted) vs Cal.diy (MIT self-host)

  • Design — Penpot as the open canvas default; Figma when partners already live there

  • Vault — Bitwarden cloud vs official self-host vs Vaultwarden

The stack map and stage defaults stitch the areas together. Product partner marketplaces stay elsewhere; this hub is for the IT skeleton every tech company ends up building anyway.

Start at the hub index or the stack map.

posts.title: MSI tables land in the generator
posts.description: msi-generator v0.2 writes real OLE2 compound files, cabinets, and core Windows Installer tables — still unsigned, no longer an empty stub.
posts.html:
msi-generator crossed the line from “skeleton that prints a message” to “file you can open in an OLE/MSI viewer.”

v0.2 writes a version-3 compound file, an uncompressed cabinet payload, and the core table set (Directory, Component, File, Feature, FeatureComponents, Property, Media, plus _Tables / _Columns and the string pool). MSIX gained multi-file payloads and placeholder assets so manifests stop lying about missing logos.

This is the engine Easy Installer’s msi / msix plugins call. It is not WiX, and we are not pretending a unsigned sample MSI is Store-ready — but the binary formats are finally real enough to iterate on.

Release: v0.2.0 · docs: component.

posts.title: Easy Installer becomes Ibex
posts.description: Install Builder EXtension — new name, logo, and OS package registries for the installer-authoring CLI.
posts.html:
Easy Installer is now Ibex (Install Builder EXtension): same job — author installer packages, emit CI, and put tools on PATH — clearer name, animal mark, and first-class installs via winget / Homebrew / Scoop.

  • CLI: ibex (v0.2 dual-ships transitional easy-installer-* release assets)

  • Install: winget install DevCentr.Ibex · brew tap dev-centr/tap && brew install ibex

  • Docs: Ibex · repo still dev-centr/easy-installer for now

Not a software catalog installer — it extends file managers and DevCentr; it does not replace winget for installing third-party apps.

posts.title: Easy Installer ships
posts.description: A CLI and Explorer menu for installer projects and Install in-place PATH — without waiting on a full MSI every time you want a tool on PATH.
posts.html:
We shipped Easy Installer: the host that turns “put this folder on PATH” and “build an installer from this tree” into something you can right-click or script.

The first beat is deliberately small. Install in-place (add to PATH) means what it says — append the folder to the user PATH, keep a ledger so you can undo, and skip the copy-into-Program-Files ritual when you are iterating on a CLI. File Explorer gets a menu for it (Win11 modern when the sparse package builds; classic cascade otherwise). Linux and macOS get file-manager actions too.

The second beat is the project file. installer.kdl plus plugins: portable zip always works; NSIS and Inno emit scripts and call their compilers when present; MSI/MSIX call msi-generator; AppImage gets a stub path on Linux. Optional designer GUIs are discoverable (plugins install-gui) instead of reinvented inside our IDE.

DevCentr picks up the same verbs — New → Installer Project, toolbar Install in-place PATH, and CLI modes — so the OS menu and the app are not two products pretending to be one.

Docs: Easy Installer (once the hub rebuilds) · releases.

Figure 1. Idealized Easy Installer project UI
Figure 2. DevCentr extension surface

posts.title: Easy Installer emits CI pipelines
posts.description: Scaffold GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Azure Pipelines, Jenkins, CircleCI, or Bitbucket workflows for installer builds — without packaging on your laptop.
posts.html:
Easy Installer now has a first-class CI pipeline intent: edit ci-runner.sdl, run emit-ci, and get runner YAML plus CI-INSTALLER.adoc (how to enable pipelines, secrets, tags, and artifact downloads). Local build stays optional for smoke tests.

Supported emitters in this cut: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Azure Pipelines, Jenkins (Declarative), CircleCI, and Bitbucket Pipelines. DevCentr’s New Installer dialog can choose CI pipeline only; Explorer gets New Installer CI pipeline… (--mode=emit-ci).

Docs: emit CI how-to · repo.

posts.title: We’re partnering with OpenShellOrg (on purpose)
posts.description: DevCentr and OpenShellOrg are locking in the sibling story—toolchain ownership on our side, shell entrypoint honesty on theirs.
posts.html:
Quick confession: for a minute we almost convinced ourselves the whole “wrong Node / wrong Flutter / wrong host” rant lived under OpenShellOrg, because that’s where the pain hits—you type a command and the wrong process runs. Then we remembered why we put Toolchain Management in DevCentr in the first place: the full lifecycle (pin, health, repair, upgrade) is an ecosystem-orchestration problem. The shell just happens to be the crime scene.

So we’re doing the grown-up thing.

DevCentr keeps the canonical Toolchain Management Pattern → Protocol → Control Plane → TCF kit. That’s the “official entrypoint owns the lifecycle” philosophy, the advisories in Ecosystem Management, the “stop telling newcomers to go shop for nvm/FVM first” stance.

OpenShellOrg keeps the shell-boundary essay: Entrypoint Dispatch — auto-install and re-exec the right host/version when the pin says so — plus nu-require, SOS, structured-shell thesis, env-refresh / shell-host plans. Complementary. Not a duplicate manifesto with a different logo.

Aligned, not merged. Cross-linked like we mean it. Footers and org profiles now show the sibling cluster so people stop spelunking.

If you want the vibe in one line: we orchestrate the workshop; they refuse to let the hammer lie about which nail it’s hitting.

Figure 1. Official toolchain architecture
Figure 2. Sibling ownership

Links worth bookmarking: OpenShellOrg, their docs, Toolchain Management Pattern, and the alignment page in general-knowledge (Dev-Centr and OpenShellOrg).

posts.title: We’re opening a News desk
posts.description: Why DevCentr is starting a public News feed—and what you won't find here.
posts.html:
Dev-Centr has been shipping in public for a while—docs, tools, the app, the whole messy orbit of related projects. What we haven’t had is a place to talk about that work like people talk about it: the why, the bets, the “here’s where we’re headed” pieces.

So we’re starting News at devcentr.org/news.

Think magazine column more than release notes. If something changes how we build, how we show up as an org, or what we’re trying to become, it belongs here. If it’s “we fixed a heading and renamed three pages,” that’s the Changelog.

We’ll write when there’s something worth saying. No weekly quota. No content mill. Subscribe to the RSS or Atom feed if you want a ping when we do.

Elsewhere, as always: the docs, the repos, and the app.

posts.title: Stop dumping people into the docs
posts.description: We built a Help hub so “I need assistance” doesn't mean “go read the manual.”
posts.html:
Here’s a quiet failure mode a lot of open projects share: someone shows up stuck, and the only door we offer is documentation. Docs are great when you want to learn. They’re a cold shoulder when you want a person—or at least a clear path to one.

So we put up a Help hub at devcentr.org/help.

The idea is simple. Help is the umbrella. Under it you can choose self-help (docs, guides, the knowledge base) or support (talk to us). Status and community channels sit next to both, so you’re not hunting through the footer for Slack or “is the site up?”

We don’t have a polished ticket desk yet—and we’re not going to pretend we do. For now, mail support@devcentr.org. A real assisted desk (tickets, maybe AI triage) is on the roadmap; we’d rather ship an honest front door than a half-built system with a shiny button.

If you just want the pulse of our public surfaces, /status runs live probes. Longer uptime history still lives at status.devcentr.org.

This is a small change on the site. It’s a bigger change in posture: we assume visitors arrive with different jobs to do, and we stop treating “read the docs” as the only answer.

posts.title: Our logo shouldn’t need a proprietary player
posts.description: Why DevCentr's new mark stays in SVG—and why we're cautious about Rive as a default for open brands.
posts.html:
We finally gave DevCentr a proper mark: an orbital hub that reads as a center of gravity. You’ll see it on the site, in the GitHub avatar, and in the motion loop that doesn’t need JavaScript to breathe.

That last part matters more than it sounds.

There’s a loud fashion in product design right now: ship brand motion as a black-box file, drop in a player, call it modern. Rive is genuinely good at interactive chrome—state machines, theme hooks, the works. Its runtimes are open. The editor isn’t, and the .riv format is binary. That means weak git diffs and a hard wall for anyone (human or agent) who wants to edit the motion as text.

We’re building an open ecosystem. Our logo shouldn’t be the one asset that only opens in a paid app.

So the default for portable marks stays animated SVG and CSS. Lottie when you’ve got a baked After Effects timeline. Rive when you’re already deep in interactive app UI and the player is justified. We’re documenting those lanes in General Knowledge; the short version is: don’t hard-advocate a proprietary editor as the open standard for brand motion.

Longer term we want something text-first that agents can actually edit. Popkorn is an early CSS-shaped candidate—interesting, not a Dev-Centr default yet. If that future interests you, there’s an open thread on rich interactivity at ayarse/popkorn#7.

The mark is the visible change. The opinion underneath it is the story: open brands should travel as open source.
